kurz: Besides the fee on the contract note, the larger part of trading costs is contained in the price, and this part too can be measured to the cent.

bloecke.md:
A securities order causes two kinds of costs. The explicit costs appear on the contract note: order fee, trading venue fee, external cost fee and currency conversion fee. The implicit costs, by contrast, appear nowhere. They are not charged as a fee and arise from a worse price. For most private investors, they make up the larger part.

The difference has practical consequences. Explicit costs are known before the order is sent and can be reduced by choosing a broker. Implicit costs only arise at the moment of execution. They depend on the instrument, the trading venue, the time of day and the size of your own order, and they do not appear in any statement. Investors who want to know them have to measure them themselves.

## Measuring the bid-ask spread

The bid-ask spread is the gap between the highest buy order (bid) and the lowest sell order (ask). An immediate purchase is executed at the ask price, an immediate sale at the bid price. The fair reference price lies in between. A single trade therefore costs half the [[Spread|spread]]. The full spread is only incurred on a round trip, that is on a purchase and a later sale.

bloecke.formel: Spread in basis points = (Ask − Bid) / Mid × 10,000
bloecke.erklaerung: A basis point is one hundredth of a per cent. The spread in basis points makes costs comparable across instruments and order sizes. A single order bears half of it.
variablen: Lowest selling price in the order book
Highest buying price in the order book
Average of the two. Nobody pays this price, yet everything is measured against it
bloecke.beispiel: With a bid of 99.98 and an ask of 100.02, the result is (0.04 / 100.00) × 10,000 = 4 basis points. A purchase costs 2 basis points of this, that is €1 per €5,000 of order volume.

bloecke.md:
However, the quoted spread is only an offer for a certain volume. Only the effective spread shows the costs actually incurred on an order. It is twice the distance between the execution price and the mid price at the moment the order was received, and is therefore directly comparable with the quoted spread. The order itself costs the single distance, that is half the effective spread. This gives a measurement method that any investor can use. Before sending the order, you note the bid and ask prices and compare them with the price on the contract note after execution. The difference gives the implicit costs of this order to the cent.

For Xetra, Deutsche Börse publishes its own indicator for this, the Xetra Liquidity Measure. It states the cost of a round-trip trade for a fixed order volume in basis points. For the largest world ETFs, spreads in the order of three to five basis points are reported during core trading hours. This order of magnitude comes from secondary sources and is not a measured daily average. Outside core trading hours, the spread becomes considerably wider.

## Order size and market impact

The best spread only applies to the number of units offered at the best price level. Anything beyond that is executed at worse prices on the following price levels of the order book. The investor portal of Deutsche Börse shows ten price levels per side with cumulative volumes for Xetra, while professional data feeds show the entire visible order book. What remains hidden is mainly the undisclosed parts of iceberg orders and the Xetra Midpoint book. For a world ETF with volumes in the millions at each level, the limit of ten levels does not matter for the order sizes of private investors, but for a small cap it does.

bloecke.titel: Ask side of a small cap in a model order book, mid between bid and ask at €24.77

bloecke.md:
A market order for 1,200 units is executed with 300 units at 24.80, 400 at 24.86 and 500 at €24.94. The contract note shows €29,854, and the average price is 24.88. Compared with the mid of 24.77, that is €130 more. Of this, €36 is due to half the spread and €94 to [[Market impact|market impact]], that is the price movement caused by your own order volume. The order fee of one euro hardly matters by comparison.

Only a limit helps against market impact. A limit order at 24.82 is executed at the first level, and the rest waits. In the process, 900 units can remain open while the price moves away from the limit. These opportunity costs of not trading are real. Unlike market impact, however, they are not systematically negative, because the price can also move towards the limit.

bloecke.titel: Cost structure of four different orders
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in basis points of the order volume. The assumptions are a €1 flat order fee, a spread of 4 basis points for the ETF during core hours, 20 basis points at off-peak times and a 0.25% conversion fee per currency leg. The row for the small cap is based on the order book above. Which type of cost predominates depends on the transaction and not on the broker.

bloecke.titel: Predominant type of cost by order volume and liquidity
bloecke.unter: The four examples give a rule of thumb: comparing fees only pays off in the top-left field.

felder.text: Savings plan contribution into a large ETF. The flat fee is high in percentage terms, the spread negligible. Here the broker matters.
Large order in a large ETF. The spread grows with the volume, the flat fee hardly at all. Here the trading venue and the time of day matter.
Small order in a small cap or niche ETF. Spreads of 1% or more are normal and more expensive than any fee.
Large order in a thin market. The order moves the price against itself. Here the only thing that matters is how patiently limits are set.

bloecke.md:
## Time of day as a cost factor

A market maker quotes prices and takes on a risk in doing so. It does not know whether the other side is better informed, and it must be able to hedge its position. The less successful it is at this, the wider it sets the spread. This explains how spreads develop over the course of the day. Continuous trading on Xetra runs from 9:00 to 17:30, and Xetra is the reference market with the highest liquidity. Tradegate BSX is open from 7:30 to 22:00, gettex and LS Exchange until 23:00. Off-exchange, Lang & Schwarz also trades on Saturdays from 10:00 to 13:00 and on Sundays from 17:00 to 19:00.

For a world ETF with a high US share, the market for the most important part of the portfolio is closed in the morning. The [[iNAV]] is recalculated every 15 to 60 seconds, but it is based on estimated prices. The market maker demands a wider spread for this uncertainty. From 15:30, the US exchanges are open, and an observed price is available instead of an estimate. Spreads are then typically at their narrowest.

On Saturdays and Sundays, all underlying markets are closed. The market maker bears the entire news risk alone until Monday morning and sets the spread correspondingly wide. There is no reference price against which the contract note could be checked. Investors who trade at the weekend pay the market maker compensation for this risk via the price, that is implicit costs that do not appear on any contract note.

## Costs of currency conversion

A US share can be bought in euros on a German trading venue or in dollars on its home exchange. The currency risk is the same in both cases, because the company's value is generated in dollars, regardless of the currency in which the price is displayed. The two routes differ in who does the conversion and how visible it is.

When buying in euros, the market maker handles the conversion and adds its margin to the price. When buying in dollars via a foreign currency account, the broker charges a conversion fee, usually as a percentage of the transaction value. It is incurred on every conversion, that is on purchase, on sale and on every dividend. The fee is only visible in the second variant. The first variant is therefore not cheaper; its costs are just harder to check.

bloecke.titel: End of order flow rebates in 2026
bloecke.md: Payment for order flow is the rebate that a trading venue paid to the broker for orders routed to it. It has been prohibited in the EU since 28 March 2024 by Article 39a MiFIR. Germany made use of the transitional option, and for German brokers the practice ended on 30 June 2026. Since then, revenue has had to come from fees, spreads, interest margins and subscription models. This eliminates a conflict of interest but does not automatically make trading cheaper. Price lists and execution quality should therefore be compared anew in 2026.

## Withholding tax on foreign dividends

Foreign dividends are taxed twice before they reach the investor. First, the source country, that is the country where the company is domiciled, deducts [[Withholding tax|withholding tax]]. Germany then levies capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer) of 25% under Section 43a(1) sentence 1 no. 1 EStG (Income Tax Act), plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge. To avoid double taxation, the custodian credits the foreign tax. However, this only applies up to the rate that the double taxation agreement grants the source country, as a rule up to 15 percentage points (Section 32d(5) EStG).

bloecke.titel: Deductions from a €100 gross dividend on a US share
bloecke.unter: Calculated under Section 32d(5) and Section 43a EStG, with treaty status on file and the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) used up, excluding church tax.

schritte.name: Capital income withholding tax 25% less 15 points credit

bloecke.md: The calculation has a little-known side effect. Because the solidarity surcharge is only levied on the remaining German capital income withholding tax, the total burden is 25.55%. A German dividend, by contrast, bears 26.375%. A withholding tax of 15% is therefore not a disadvantage. A disadvantage only arises from withholding tax above the creditable 15 points.

bloecke.titel: Amount credited from a €100 gross dividend by source country (excluding church tax, allowance used up)

bloecke.md: Withholding tax above the creditable 15 points can only be reclaimed by application; for Swiss shares, 20 percentage points are reclaimed via a form from the Swiss Federal Tax Administration (ESTV). This is why the domicile of a fund also matters. An Irish fund bears 15% instead of 30% withholding tax on US dividends. With a US dividend yield of 1.6%, this adds around 0.24 percentage points of return a year. This only becomes visible in the [[Tracking difference|tracking difference]], never in the management fee.

As long as the saver's allowance of €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG) covers the income for the whole year, no German capital income withholding tax is due. The foreign withholding tax then cannot be credited against any tax. A US gross dividend of €100 thus becomes €85 instead of €100. The order in which income arises during the year does not matter. The bank records uncredited withholding tax in a withholding tax pot (Quellensteuertopf) and credits it against capital income withholding tax that is still incurred in the same calendar year, even if that tax relates to domestic income.

## Costs of rebalancing

A portfolio of €100,000 contains 70% equities and 30% bonds. In one year, equities return 15% and bonds 3%. Afterwards, the equity portion stands at €80,500 and the bond portion at €30,900, a total of €111,400. The target allocation requires €77,980 in equities. So equities worth €2,520 have to be sold and bonds bought for the same amount.

The transaction costs consist of two flat order fees of €1 each and half the spread of 0.04% on €2,520 for each trade. Together that comes to around €4.02.

For the tax, it is assumed that 40% of the sale proceeds are capital gain, that is €1,008. After the 30% [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]] for equity funds (Section 20(1) InvStG, Investment Tax Act), €705.60 remains taxable. At 26.375%, that results in €186.10 in tax.

The tax is therefore forty-six times the trading costs. When rebalancing, a fee comparison only reduces the smaller of the two cost blocks.

If, on the other hand, the saver's allowance were otherwise unused in the same year, the €705.60 would fall below it, and the tax would be zero. The same rebalancing therefore costs between €4 and €190, depending on the other capital income in the calendar year.

As long as you keep paying in, the target allocation can be restored via the next savings contributions. With a monthly contribution of €250, the €2,520 shortfall in the bond portion is made up after just over 14 contributions that go entirely into bonds instead of equities. Each contribution reduces the shortfall by only €175, because €75 of it belongs in bonds anyway according to the target allocation. The realised gain is zero. This works as long as the inflow is large enough relative to the deviation. With a large portfolio and a small contribution, at some point it is no longer sufficient. Then selling makes more sense than letting the allocation deviate from the target permanently.

A position of €50,000 in a world ETF contains €20,000 of unrealised gains. A competing product has a management fee that is 0.05 percentage points lower. The switch therefore appears to be a pure cost optimisation.

- Tax due immediately: 20,000 × 70% (after partial exemption) × 26.375% = €3,692.50.
- Annual saving: 0.05% of around €50,000 = €25.
- In purely arithmetical terms, it takes around 150 years for the saving to offset the tax.

The calculation exaggerates, because the tax would have been due anyway on a later sale. Strictly speaking, only the tax deferral effect is lost, that is the return that the tax amount would have earned until the later sale. Even this effect is greater than €25 a year over any realistic investment horizon. The situation is different only if there is hardly any unrealised gain or if the tracking difference of the old product has been systematically worse for years, and not just its fee higher.

Four types of cost, in descending order of how often they are underestimated: the realised tax when rebalancing, market impact for thinly traded securities, half the spread at an unfavourable time of day and currency conversion on every single transaction. The order fee comes fifth and is the only type of cost that brokers feature in their advertising.

1. Before sending the order, note the bid and ask prices and the time. The mid between the two prices is the reference price.
2. After execution, compare the price on the contract note with this mid: for a purchase, (Execution − Mid) / Mid × 10,000 gives the implicit costs in basis points; for a sale, (Mid − Execution) / Mid × 10,000 applies.
3. Add the explicit costs from the contract note, also in basis points of the volume.
4. Repeat the measurement over ten orders and take the average, because some individual deviations also turn out in the investor's favour. Only the average shows whether the costs come from the price list or from your own trading habits.

mitnehmen: Explicit costs appear on the contract note; implicit costs are contained in the price and are higher for most orders.
A trade costs half the spread, and any quantity beyond the best price level causes additional market impact.
Which type of cost predominates depends on the combination of order size and liquidity and not on the broker.
Foreign withholding tax is creditable up to 15 percentage points (Section 32d(5) EStG); beyond that, only an application helps, and without German tax no credit is possible.
When rebalancing and when switching products, the realised tax is almost always the largest cost block, often by a factor of 40 or more.

begriffe.text: Costs that are not charged as a fee and arise from a worse price. They include half the spread, market impact and delay costs. They do not appear in any fee statement.

Twice the distance between the execution price achieved and the mid between bid and ask at the moment the order is received. It is the only indicator that measures the actual costs of a specific order. The order itself bears half of it.

Price movement that an order triggers through its own volume when it uses up several price levels of the order book. Market impact grows disproportionately with order size and falls as liquidity rises.

Tax withheld directly by the country in which the distributing company is domiciled. In Germany, it is creditable against the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) up to the rate provided for in the double taxation agreement, usually 15 percentage points (Section 32d(5) EStG). A refund of the remainder must be applied for in the source country.
Restoring the target allocation by distributing new contributions instead of selling. No gains are realised, so the largest cost block of rebalancing does not arise.
